text:
🚀 Cracked Accenture Data Engineer Interview (0–5 YOE)
A few months back, I was debugging pipelines & doubting myself.
 Last week, I got the “Congratulations! You’re selected” mail from Accenture 💙
Here’s the breakdown 👇
⚙️ Round 1 – SQL
💬 Question: Find employees earning more than avg salary in their department.

SELECT e.name, e.salary 
FROM employees e 
WHERE salary > (
 SELECT AVG(salary) 
 FROM employees 
 WHERE department_id = e.department_id
);
✅ Tip: Know your joins, CTEs, and window functions cold.
🧠 Round 2 – Data Pipeline
💬 Question: How would you design a pipeline for daily sales data?
 💡 Answer:
 “Use ADF for orchestration, PySpark for transform, Snowflake for storage.”
 ✅ Tip: Think architecture + monitoring, not just tools.
🧩 Round 3 – PySpark
💬 Question: Top 3 products sold in each region?

windowSpec = Window.partitionBy("region").orderBy(col("sales").desc())
df.withColumn("rank", rank().over(windowSpec)).filter(col("rank") <= 3)

author: Jaydeep Patel
headline: Consultant Data & AI @ Deloitte USI, Analyst @ HCLTech, Data Engineer
text:
🚀 Netflix Data Analyst Interview Experience (24 LPA)

A friend recently shared their Netflix Data Analyst interview journey, and it was one of the most exciting yet challenging processes — focused on analytical thinking, storytelling, and product sense.

Here’s a complete breakdown 👇

🔹 Round 1 – SQL + Case Analysis
1️⃣ Find the top 5 most-watched shows per region.
2️⃣ Calculate churn rate using monthly subscriber data.
3️⃣ Identify peak viewing hours per day from a large log dataset.
4️⃣ Case: “How would you analyze the success of a newly released Netflix series?”

🔹 Round 2 – Product + Statistics Round
5️⃣ Explain A/B testing — how would you test a new recommendation algorithm?
6️⃣ How do you define a good metric for user engagement on Netflix?
7️⃣ Estimate daily bandwidth savings if compression improves by 15%.

🔹 Round 3 – Dashboard + Storytelling
8️⃣ Build a dashboard that tracks content performance over time (Power BI/Tableau).
9️⃣ Present an insight-driven story: “Which genre is driving retention and why?”
🔟 Suggest improvements to Netflix’s content recommendation based on your analysis.

💡 Key Tip: Netflix looks for data-driven storytellers who can blend numbers with narratives. Focus on impact over execution.

🔥 Prepare smartly — great storytelling = great analytics!

author: Abilasha Veeraraghavan
headline: I design learning moments
text:
Trigger warning: Death, healing 

Back in 2019, death entered my home without offering the grace of a single warning.

I was neck-deep in work at office when I got a sudden call.
I had lost my mom.
What’s worse is that I had just spoken to her half an hour earlier. She was her usual chirpy self.

I was 21, new to the corporate world, and absolutely lost.
But this post isn’t about grief.
It’s about empathy.

I had just been onboarded onto a mega project with tight deadlines.
But my manager didn’t care about that.
She cared about me.

She gave me a month off with no questions asked.
She even came home to pay her respects, hugged me tight for 15 minutes.
She told my team: “Do not disturb her at any cost.”
And they didn’t.
They covered for me, checked on me every day, and made sure I could just… breathe.

That month officially became my crash course in adulthood.
I learned how to make a cup of tea without staining the kitchen walls.
Figured out what groceries we actually needed.
Discovered that “atta” isn’t just flour. It comes in multiple variants (some of which are totally useless, by the way!)
Realized that milk packets do, in fact, expire.
I was learning to manage a home, run errands... and somehow, keep myself together.

But even through all that chaos, I could almost hear my mom laughing, nudging me to find the good in everything.

And so I did.
Every little disaster became a lesson. Every small win, a reason to smile.

That phase changed how I saw workplaces and people.
Today, whenever I lead a proposal, project, or a team, I try to be that person.
The one who covers for others.
The one who makes space for someone to just be human.

People often ask, “Why do you go above and beyond for others?”
Because someone once did that for me, while I tried to navigate the unknown.
And that made all the difference. :)
